body.narration: Start with the rendering pipeline. The vertex function works on geometry. Rasterization turns triangles into covered fragments. The fragment function computes surface values. That is our map: inputs, a calculation, then a visible result.
body.motion: Quad corners move, then the triangle fills with fragment cells.
body.why: A flat mesh preserves the actual relationship between vertices and coverage; an isometric conveyor obscures it.

body.narration: Godot uses its own shading language, closely related to G L S L. Save it as dot G D shader. Shader type selects the context. Canvas item serves two D; spatial serves three D.
body.motion: Reveal shader_type first; then the processor function.
body.why: The executed minimal file makes the structure immediately readable.

body.narration: Other shader contexts include particles, sky, and fog. Not every context exposes the same processor functions or built-ins. Older Godot three tutorials use dot shader files. In Godot, vertex and fragment replace the usual G L S L main entry point.
body.motion: Focus the actual language reference while identifying context-dependent behavior.
body.why: The real reference gives students the place to check their shader context.

body.narration: Select a drawable node, open Material, and assign a ShaderMaterial. That material holds a Shader resource. Here the real editor shows our ColorRect with the material attached. Open its shader to edit the program.
body.motion: Start at the scene tree, then focus the actual Material field.
body.why: A real editor capture exists; it establishes the actual node and material wiring.

body.narration: This is a complete first shader. Void means the function returns no ordinary value. Instead, it writes COLOR. Four components specify red, green, blue, and opacity. One in the last component means fully opaque.
body.motion: Reveal COLOR assignment after the function shell.
body.why: Students need the exact runnable syntax before inspecting the result.

body.narration: Every covered fragment receives the same four numbers, so the whole rectangle becomes pink. This output came from Godot. No texture coordinates appear in the calculation, so there is no reason for one part to differ.
body.motion: Ring the center, then the edge of the same uniform patch.
body.why: Actual pixels verify the executable example without inventing output.

body.narration: For a three D material, write ALBEDO for the base color. The lighting system uses it along with properties such as roughness and the surface normal. ALBEDO is a three-component vector; opacity has its own output.
body.motion: Reveal ALBEDO, then ROUGHNESS; retain the spatial declaration.
body.why: Exact tested shader source ties the material outputs to code.

body.narration: In a spatial shader, ALPHA controls opacity. This small example writes zero point three. Defining light lets you customize lighting where that processor is supported; you do not need an empty light function in every shader.
body.motion: Reveal the independent ALPHA output after ALBEDO.
body.why: The exact program sets up the following real opaque and transparent comparison.

body.narration: Here is the rendered cube. Writing ALPHA as zero point three makes a transparent surface. That alone does not create physically convincing glass. Refraction, lighting, and transparency sorting are separate questions.
body.motion: Reveal the opaque render, then the actual alpha render beside it.
body.why: A paired comparison exposes the limit of the transcript’s glass analogy.

body.narration: Now coordinates. In a two D vertex function, VERTEX gives a local position. Add twenty to its horizontal component and the drawn geometry shifts right. Use twenty point zero because that component is a float.
body.motion: Reveal VERTEX.x and its increment.
body.why: The exact built-in and floating literal are the teaching target here.

body.narration: Before it moves, predict what happens to the collider. The drawn square shifts; the collision outline stays put. A shader changes rendering. It does not move the node or rewrite your physics shape.
body.motion: Hold the initial aligned square and collider, then move only the filled square.
body.why: The labeled conceptual overlay exposes a distinction a still cannot show.

body.narration: TIME is an engine clock. Feeding it into sine makes the offset oscillate. Each frame recomputes the offset from the supplied time. We are not accumulating the previous frame’s vertex position.
body.motion: Reveal amplitude, then the sine expression.
body.why: The exact expression shows that time is an input rather than stored position.

body.narration: A clock value of zero, then a quarter turn, then a half turn produces zero offset, maximum offset, then zero again. For an event like damage, drive your own uniform from game state instead of treating TIME as an event timer.
body.motion: A clock marker advances while one quad shifts and returns.
body.why: A schematic clock isolates the dependency; captures would confound wall time.

body.narration: UV gives texture coordinates for the current point. This example places U into red and V into green. Blue stays zero. We are turning an invisible coordinate field into something we can inspect.
body.motion: Reveal UV inside the vec4 constructor.
body.why: Runnable color encoding connects the conceptual field to shader syntax.

body.narration: On this rectangle, the upper left is dark. Move right and red increases. Move down and green increases. The lower right combines both. The gradient is many invocations applying one rule to different inputs.
body.motion: Camera focuses upper left, then lower right; no camera transition across midpoint.
body.why: The actual Godot gradient proves the mapping used by this example.

body.narration: Do not picture a paintbrush remembering the last pixel. Each fragment has local inputs and local work. Other pixels can be read through appropriate textures, but you cannot rely on the neighboring invocation having already finished.
body.motion: All cells receive their own coordinate marker; erase the imagined serial arrow.
body.why: A grid of actual fragment locations is more direct than a physical factory metaphor.

body.narration: Types make the calculation explicit. Bool holds true or false. Int holds an integer. Float holds a real-valued approximation. Statements end in semicolons. Convert an integer deliberately when a calculation needs a float.
body.motion: Reveal bool, int, then the explicit float constructor.
body.why: Exact declarations are the evidence and the usable pattern.

body.narration: Here is a deliberate failure: assigning the integer literal five directly to a float. Godot reports a type error. Five point zero or an explicit float conversion fixes it. Read the shader diagnostics, not just the process exit status.
body.motion: Show the exact invalid line followed by the actual compiler diagnostic.
body.why: Recorded local diagnostics test the claim rather than merely repeat it.

body.narration: A vector groups components. These four numbers can be addressed as X, Y, Z, W, or as red, green, blue, alpha. The names change with your interpretation; the underlying four values do not.
body.motion: Four fixed cells keep their values while component labels switch.
body.why: Stable cells make aliasing visible before syntax grows.

body.narration: Swizzling selects and reorders components. B G R reverses the three color channels. X X copies the first component into a two-component vector. Match the result’s size, and never mix naming families inside one swizzle.
body.motion: Reveal c.bgr, then c.xx; keep the original vector visible.
body.why: The exact tested forms prevent the transcript’s mistaken vec2/three-component example.

body.narration: A matrix constructor takes columns. Put one and two in the first column, three and four in the second. Multiplying by the first basis vector selects that first column: one, two. It does not select the first row.
body.motion: Two column vectors assemble into a matrix; highlight the first column as output.
body.why: The column-versus-row misconception requires spatial arrangement.

body.narration: Here is that calculation in shader code. Matrix indexing also starts with the column. The result is divided by four only to fit this color demonstration. The colored output is a diagnostic encoding, not a new matrix rule.
body.motion: Reveal matrix constructor then matrix-vector multiplication and display scaling.
body.why: The source distinguishes the mathematical result from its color encoding.

body.narration: An array stores several values of the same type. Its first index is zero. These three weights live at indices zero, one, and two. Index one selects zero point three. Keep every access inside the array’s bounds.
body.motion: Reveal the array, then the weights[1] access.
body.why: Small exact code preserves the declaration and indexing syntax.

body.narration: Now make the material adjustable. A uniform supplies a value shared by the invocations using that material. Source color gives a color control; hint range gives a numeric control. The shader reads those values while it runs.
body.motion: Reveal the two uniform declarations before their use.
body.why: The declarations expose the type, hint, default, and scope without small Inspector text.

body.narration: An enum hint names integer choices. A range hint guides the Inspector, but it does not enforce a runtime bound. Our local test stored seven in a parameter whose suggested range was zero to one. Clamp when the effect requires it.
body.motion: Reveal enum declaration, set_shader_parameter excerpt, then the recorded value.
body.why: Exact source plus captured output separates the editor convenience from runtime validation.

body.narration: Predict what happens when two nodes share this ShaderMaterial and we change its tint. Both become orange. The value belongs to the shared material resource, so duplicating a node does not automatically give it independent parameters.
body.motion: Reveal both patches, then ring their identical colors.
body.why: Real output demonstrates the shared-resource consequence more directly than an ownership metaphor.

body.narration: One fix is a separate material resource. The two materials can still share the same shader program. Here only one tint changes. You need different parameter storage, not another copy of the shader’s source code.
body.motion: Move the focus from orange left to blue right.
body.why: The actual run proves independence; narration supplies the resource relationship.

body.narration: Another option is an instance uniform, supported for canvas item and spatial shaders in the stable reference checked here. Set it on each drawable node. The material stays shared while the tint varies. Check support in your project’s version.
body.motion: Reveal instance uniform, then show the node setter excerpt.
body.why: Literal tested syntax plus setter is the useful distinction.

body.narration: A sampler binds a texture. Texture reads sample that image at supplied coordinates. Here image tex is the input and UV is the address. Use source color for color textures; a data map has a different role.
body.motion: Reveal sampler declaration, then texture(image_tex, UV).
body.why: Exact sampling syntax is needed before inspecting the captured checkerboard.

body.narration: This checkerboard is a real texture sample. On a Sprite, sampling TEXTURE directly reads the texture alone. Incoming COLOR already includes the normal texture and vertex-color contribution. Choose deliberately, or your effect can discard tint and modulation.
body.motion: Zoom to a checker boundary to show that sampling chooses image values.
body.why: The capture establishes sampling; the distinction is carried into the later COLOR-preserving effect.

body.narration: A varying carries data between stages. Here the vertex function writes horizontal from U. The fragment function reads it. This is stage-to-stage transport, not a variable storing yesterday’s frame or a neighbor’s output.
body.motion: Reveal varying declaration, writer, then reader.
body.why: Exact stage functions expose who writes and reads the value.

body.narration: The endpoints carry zero and one. Between them, rasterization interpolates the value. Halfway across this flat rectangle, the value is about one half. That is why a few vertex values can create a smooth fragment gradient.
body.motion: Two endpoint values persist while an interpolated ramp grows between them.
body.why: Animation explains where the in-between values come from.

body.narration: Ordinary conditionals work inside the shader. This example chooses dark on the left and light on the right by comparing U with one half. The decision is local to each invocation, so different fragments take different branches.
body.motion: Reveal the condition before the two branch assignments.
body.why: The actual source is small enough to make local control flow explicit.

body.narration: A switch selects an integer case. Here mode one produces one quarter. Break stops execution from continuing into later cases. Include explicit breaks in the demonstrated version, including the default branch.
body.motion: Reveal the selected case and its break, then the other cases.
body.why: The tested syntax matters; this excerpt keeps all cases readable.

body.narration: Remove the first two breaks and mode one keeps going: one quarter, then three quarters, then one tenth. The captured outputs differ. The language accepted the program; the control flow still changed the meaning.
body.motion: Trace the three values in order; reveal the two real output patches side by side.
body.why: A trace plus actual rendered difference makes the bug concrete.

body.narration: A loop needs a clear stopping condition and progress toward it. This one visits three weights, advances its index, and adds them to one. Keeping the bound small also keeps the work per fragment understandable.
body.motion: Reveal initialization, bound, increment, then addition.
body.why: Students need a complete working for-loop they can copy safely.

body.narration: Watch the index: zero, one, two, then stop at three. A while loop also needs progress. A missing increment can hang rendering. We inspect that failure in a trace; we do not freeze the editor to prove it.
body.motion: Cursor advances through three array cells and lands at a stop marker; missing-progress branch stays unexecuted.
body.why: A bounded trace teaches the failure without intentionally hanging the GPU.

body.narration: Put the pieces together. Preserve incoming COLOR, blend its RGB toward a tint, and keep its alpha. Clamp the amount between zero and one. That makes the input contract explicit even when game code sends an unexpected value.
body.motion: Reveal base preservation, mix with clamp, and base.a.
body.why: The complete tested effect is the reusable student artifact.

body.narration: Before looking, predict three settings. Zero should preserve the base. One should reach the tint. One half should lie between them. These are the actual rendered samples. Transparent artwork needs a separate alpha check too.
body.motion: Hold the three labeled settings, then inspect each patch in order.
body.why: Native Godot output tests the prediction under a stated renderer.

body.narration: A parser check is useful, but a rendered image answers a different question. Our test inspects shader errors and selected pixels. It does not prove performance on every device or whether this color communicates danger well in your game.
body.motion: Recorded verification lines arrive; separate numerical checks from visual judgment.
body.why: The recorded local report makes the evidence boundary auditable.

body.narration: Use the stable documentation for first two D and first three D shaders. Then keep the language reference nearby. If you know G L S L, use the migration guide. Match documentation to your installed release.
body.motion: Push into the real tutorial heading and introduction.
body.why: The live documentation is shown as itself, with exact links in the companion.

body.narration: The Book of Shaders teaches the mathematical habits: coordinate fields, shaping functions, patterns, and noise. Its examples use plain G L S L. Translate the entry points and inputs into Godot rather than pasting every example unchanged.
body.motion: Move from the real title to the contents list.
body.why: The actual resource is recognizable and the transfer limitation is explicit.

body.narration: Godot Shaders is a community library. Choose a small effect, check its Godot version and license, and change one parameter at a time. Predict the visible difference before running it. Reading a shader is active experimentation.
body.motion: Focus the actual shader gallery after establishing the site.
body.why: A real capture avoids inventing library entries or claiming all examples are compatible.

body.narration: Visual Shaders offer a graph editor for building these programs. Nodes change the authoring interface; they do not remove the need to understand coordinates, types, and data flow. Use the form that helps you inspect the calculation.
body.motion: Camera moves into the real VisualShader documentation and its node-graph example.
body.why: The official real interface image keeps the tool recognizable without a fake session.

body.narration: Compute shaders use raw G L S L through RenderingDevice. They are a separate low-level path for general GPU work. The official tutorial requires a RenderingDevice renderer, such as Forward Plus or Mobile, rather than Compatibility.
body.motion: Focus the actual renderer requirement, then the compute code.
body.why: The actual prerequisite prevents promising compute in this Compatibility lab.

body.narration: Keep one loop: predict a visible change, alter one input, run the engine, and compare the result. If the result surprises you, inspect the type, coordinates, and ownership of that input before adding more code.
body.motion: A single patch persists through predicted, changed, rendered, and compared states.
body.why: One persistent surface keeps attention on the controlled experiment rather than an abstract production process.
